utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, and our case manager, Mrs. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. Madam Vidovic, appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts. Good morning also to my learned friends from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to you and your team. As you have -- may have noticed I thought may have -- you surely noticed there is our colleague Judge Eser missing today. For justified urgent personal reasons, he cannot be with us and he won't be with us today and tomorrow, so we have had recourse to Rule 15 bis and it's paragraph A which authorises the remaining judges of the Chamber to decide that the hearing of the case could continue in the absence of that judge for a period of not more than five working days. As you know, we are only sitting today and tomorrow this week, so we decided to proceed, particularly considering that this witness has already been here and sent home around about Easter he was here, and in fact the first thing that I will do is to explain to him and also apologise to him. So any preliminaries? Apart from the fact that you hope you have not forgotten that we have a meeting in my room at 10.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring the witness in, and as I made it clear last Thursday, you've got today and not more than today, and Defence has got tomorrow and not more than tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Professor Brkic. And welcome to this Tribunal. As you may have noticed I'm speaking in English and what I am saying and what others will be saying in English will be translated to you by our very able interpreters into your own language. I want to confirm therefore first and foremost that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If at any time during the proceedings there is faulty interpretation in the sense that it's not reaching you, or the level -- sound level is uncomfortable, please let us know immediately and we will address the problem and try to find a solution. You are very soon going to start giving evidence. Our rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in which you declare that -- solemnly, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please take a chair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers will go first for the Prosecution. The examination-in-chief is expected to last the whole of today -- of this session, of this sitting, and then tomorrow, she will be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is lead counsel for Naser Oric. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I would like to inform you of two things first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before -- I apologise to you, Ms. Sellers. Also, Professor Brkic, it's the first thing I wanted to tell you as soon as you were seated but for a moment I forgot. You have been here already waiting to testify around about our Easter. Unfortunately things went wrong at that period of time. We had planned one thing, and you are a lawyer, you know how things sometimes go a different direction, and unfortunately we could not hear your testimony at the time when you had taken the trouble to come over and make yourself available. I wish to tell you how much we appreciate the fact that you have returned and how sorry we are that we put you through all that inconvenience. On behalf of my two colleagues, Judge Eser, who is not here today because of some problems, and Judge Brydensholt from Denmark and on my own behalf and on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I would like to apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Once again good morning, Your Honour. I would like to state here in open court that we have informed the Defence this morning that we would be using an additional exhibit P325, in addition to that, that we would like to use something that has not been marked as a Prosecution exhibit yet, and I've explained to the Defence that unfortunately we do not have B/C/S translations. We will be handing that out and I certainly will entertain any delay on the part of the Defence in terms of using that document until they've had ample opportunity, if needed, to study it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Will both documents be available on Sanction for us, 315 in particular?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, they will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your position, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have accepted this and Ms. Sellers and I indeed have an agreement for this document to be delivered to us during the first break. In the English version, I believe that the B/C/S copy will be made available in the course of the day so that we can consult with our client and prepare for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for your cooperation, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which I must say has never been faulty. It has always been forthcoming and I can assure you if the day comes when your client has to be sentenced, all these acts of cooperation will be taken into consideration. Examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brkic. Could you please, for the record, just state your complete name.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Musir Brkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, would you just confirm for the Trial Chamber that you trained at the JNA military academy in Belgrade and graduated in July 1970?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: From October 1966 until the 20th of July 1970, I completed a four-year programme at the military academy, a programme for infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also could you also confirm to the Trial Chamber that you're a graduate of the faculty of law in Belgrade and what year you graduated?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the General Dzemal Bijedic faculty of law in Mostar in 1976. I had started my studies at the law school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you please also confirm that you were the deputy military prosecutor of the 7th army in Sarajevo in the summer of 1981?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: From July 1971 to midway through 1985, yes, I was the deputy military prosecutor of the 7th army district of -- military district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also likewise I would like you to confirm that you received your Ph.D. at the university of Banja Luka in March of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: On the 7th -- rather the 10th of March, 1989, I received my Ph.D. at the Djuro Pucar Stari university of Banja Luka, the law school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on February -- in February 1988 isn't it true that you were transferred to Tuzla as a military attorney and you worked as a chief of the legal section for the 7th -- 17th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction. I took up my duties as the chief military Defence counsel, and I was also the chief of the legal administration sector of the 17th Corps of the JNA. I was defending the interests of the state in matters relating to property ownership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in April of 1992, did you offer your assistance to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, I went to get a medical examination at military hospital in Sarajevo. It was supposed to be a general examination. I was facing -- I was suffering from some health problems, but on that day the demonstrations in Sarajevo had already begun, so that from the 4th until the 23rd of April, I was on leave at the military hospital in Sarajevo and I never returned to the JNA at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then volunteer or join the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I volunteered. On the 8th of April, I offered my services to the BH government, just in case they needed my assistance in my capacity as an officer and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time, were you in any type of military formation or did you hold any rank?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. Not at the time. I was not a member of any military establishment. This was a civilian Defence Ministry that I offered my services to. I held no rank in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I still had my rank of Lieutenant Colonel from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now on August 11, is that when you went to the Ministry of Defence to commence working?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 11th of April, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also confirm that on the 16th of April 1992 that you then went to the Presidency building and started to commencing work there?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: From the 16th of April to the 28th of August, 1992, I spent this whole time at the building of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I started working pursuant to their instructions and requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Trial Chamber what was your function, what type of work were you doing, in the Office of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In those days on the 11th of April 1992, I called the Defence Minister, Mr. Jerko Dzoko and told him that I was making my services available to him and my assistance for the Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There had already been the first division between the Bosniak component and the other components. He told me to get in touch with the deputy Defence Minister, Munib Bisic, who was in charge of the Bosniak component. By the time I called, by the time I got in touch, I had been vetted probably. It was still peacetime, and they sent me to what used to be the building of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at Marijin Dvor - this is the skyscraper that burned down later on - on the 11th floor they gave me a room, an office and that's where I stayed for three consecutive days. They had tasked me with producing a law on military court and a law on military prosecutors and also a law -- draft law on military courts. After I finished that I was sent back home and told to wait until I was again called. If you want me to continue, I waited for four or five days. Four or five days later on the 16th of April, 1992, I went back to the Presidency building and was told to report to the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the person who was the commander at the time, Mr. Hasan Efendic. He assigned me as his assistant for legal matters in what was then the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He gave me an office on the third floor of the Presidency. On that day and in those days, I was alone on the third floor and there must have been over 100 officers there. I was alone on the third floor of that building. There was no one else. So I went through the laws again, the draft laws, that I had produced some days before, and certain people started getting in touch with me, people who were either lawyers or from the former JNA but lawyers by profession, and they offered their help in revising and drafting these regulations and setting up all the legal services and other such tasks. As the number of people involved increased, it became clear after a while who would be the assistant of the TO Staff Commander for legal and religion-related issues and who my boss would be. As far as I remember, I was told to bring together those people who had got in touch with me and start producing all the provisions and regulations that are necessary for the proper functioning of a military force. From those days, which means mid-April, to the 13th of August 1992, if my memory serves, when the last provisions were adopted, the last laws which together comprised a whole set of laws that were sufficient for the proper functioning of a military force, we worked round the clock, all those days. For two or three months, we continued working round the clock in order to draw up the necessary drafts of all the documents that we had been requested to prepare for the Bosnian authorities. In the early days, of course, we had no regulations from the former Yugoslavia because those offices were land surveyors' offices, and there were no copies of documents around that could have been used as a blueprint to draft any laws. That would only happen two or three months later. Units came to a military library and took away some documents. So that at a later date, we could use them more by way of having [unintelligible] experience. I must say that I have a very extensive experience and I know my subject. I also studied a very peculiar subject for my Ph.D., and I had to go through a great many regulations governing the work of the armed forces and the legal service of the armed forces. I was quite familiar with the military regulations. My apologies. I may be speaking a bit too fast so my apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, yes, I would ask you two things, please slow down because we do have interpretation, but the others I just want to confirm again that on the 1st of June 1992 your position was affirmed or regularised as the chief of legal administration and general affairs in the section of the Ministry of Defence; is that correct? Now during the time -- you have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period that you were writing the various rules or regulation, did you have a staff that worked with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there was just a skeleton staff, you might say, both men and women from the former JNA, and later, the number increased. Therefore at the end, in early 1993, and throughout 1993, I had about 17 lawyers and other staff, typists, and clerks. That was at the then headquarters of the General Staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, excuse me, could I ask you, did you personally write some of the rules and regulations that would then apply to any of the armed forces or fighting forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: If you look at the overall number of all the laws and decree laws at the time, which were applied in wartime and were later confirmed in 1994, I drafted about 90 per cent of all those rules and regulations, and was the author of most of those. The rules governing the registration of motor vehicles, for example, were drafted by a different section, but with the assistance of the legal service. That means myself and my colleagues. There were some rules from the security area that were not drafted by my service, nor did we have any insight into what exactly was being done in that department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brkic, those rules that pertain to armed forces or military members, if you did not draft those, those that came out of your department, did you supervise or edit or in any way maintain some type of official control over the issuing of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Each and every document, quite literally, passed through my hands and it can be said that I drafted all these documents, regardless of the fact that it was actually my subordinates or people who worked within my department. Final approval and endorsement always had to be given by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And one other point of clarification: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, in terms of the chronological order of the documents or rules that you drafted, were they drafted in succession or were they drafted, let's say, at one time and then given chronological dates, or were they drafted based upon any scheme that had been set forward to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Given what I have said so far, given my knowledge of the army, I knew from the experience that I had with the previous army what it was that an armed force should have in order to have all the legal background for operation. That is why on our desks we had all the laws simultaneously. For example, laws and decrees -- decree laws, books of regulations and other regulations that were immediately connected with the legal support to the armed forces. So we worked on all the regulations simultaneously. The chronological order of their adoption by the Presidency, however, was different. It happened at different times. It depended on the approval of various ministries because some of these regulations had to be approved by other ministries, which had been prescribed by the constitution and other laws. It was prescribed that some documents had to be approved by various ministries because some of the regulations dealt with various areas. For example, some of our laws prescribed the ways of health care was regulated. Since we were not competent and we were not supposed to deal with that part, we had to send our law for approval to the ministry of health, and finally, after their approval, our law would become an integral legal document. After that, all the laws were coordinated. I'm talking about the draft laws which were coordinated, so in one room, there were people working on one law. In the other room, there were people working on another law. But I coordinated and authored all of these laws so there was a lot of coordination. The only difference we're dealing with is the time when the laws were adopted by the Presidency. However, in practical terms, all the laws and all the legal documents were drafted during that period of three months, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time period, while the laws were being coordinated, was it the intent of the legal section to make sure that those laws were harmonious, that they were consistent with each other as opposed to being inconsistent with each other?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was our main desire that neither the laws nor competences clashed. Our obligations that we had - and that arose from the civilian laws on the adoption of the regulations of the former Yugoslavia in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as republican laws - were strictly applied to other laws that we drafted. As far as I know, there were no collisions, maybe some things remained unsaid or uncovered. But as far as I remember, there were no collisions amongst these laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you started your duties on the 16th of April, in terms of -- I'm sorry, the 11th of April in terms of drafting, did you have to familiarise yourself with any decrees, laws or legal documents that had been issued by the newly independent Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: It was a very difficult time, and none of these regulations were published at the time. Only two regulations, one of them the decision on renaming the Territorial Defence Staff of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by deleting the word "socialist" from that name, as well as the decree law on the removal of the former commander and the appointment of a new commander are the only two laws that I was aware of. I did not see them at the time. However, subsequently I saw them in the Official Gazettes. I also saw people who were appointed but I never knew at the time how they had been appointed, by what mechanism. And after that, if I may allow -- if I may continue, when I was appointed to the duty that I since then occupied, my colleagues and myself started looking for these basic documents, and the first Official Gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we saw were issues number 1 and number 2 of that gazette, and in those we could see what were the regulations of the former Yugoslavia that were adopted as regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from then on were used as regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, we could see which regulations of the former Yugoslavia were no longer applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina as of the date of the publication of these two issues of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like the witness to be shown P286, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're referring to this decree law on the adoption of the books of regulations on the service or the decree law on defence. Which law are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I was just about to say I'm referring to the decree law on taking over the law on services in the armed forces, the application. Now in the English version it's at the bottom of the first page and will continue on the second page. Now, Mr. Brkic, is this what you're referring to in terms of some of the prior laws that you were familiarising yourself with upon taking on your services?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. No. This is not the decree. I was referring to the decree law on taking over laws and other regulations of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which were to be applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina as republican laws, and I found this in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, issue number 2/92. This decree law lists all the laws of the former Yugoslavia which were taken over by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and as of the date of publication, these laws were to be considered laws and regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within those laws that were taken over, was the federal Criminal Code incorporated into the new laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Although I was not involved in that, I can confirm that this decree law on taking over Yugoslav laws with certain amendments and supplements, the penal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted as the penal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, to be more precise, the name was the penal code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taken over as the republican law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was the formulation. This was the wording.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you would look at this decree that I've placed in front of you, the decree on the law on service in the armed forces, would you look at that briefly and tell the Trial Chamber whether you're familiar with this decree.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the number of this decree law, it was signed on the 18th of April, which is before I joined the armed forces, before I offered my services to the armed forces. This decree law was drafted by unskilled people, people who were not professionals, and it says here that the law on service in the armed forces was adopted. However, during that period of time there were no armed forces in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What I'm saying is that a law was taken over to be applied on to something that didn't exist. Secondly, only a few articles of the law were left by this decree law. As soon as I spotted this shortcoming, that was when I assumed my duties in the Ministry of Defence, the first law that we drafted was the decree law on the armed forces, and in its Article 42, as far as I can remember, we prescribed that this decree law was made null and void because it was impossible to apply and its application, in practical terms, lasted no longer than a month and a half. The application of this particular decree law that was adopted previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to describe for the Trial Chamber at that point what would have been the armed forces or fighting members or a substitution for the armed forces that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Up to the 6th of April 1992, in the so-called or the ex-Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a component of the armed forces of Yugoslavia which was called the Territorial Defence. It existed on the so-called territorial principle. If I tell you that the armed forces of Yugoslavia had two components, of which one was the Yugoslav People's Army and the other one was the Territorial Defence, then you have to know that on the 6th of April, the Territorial Defence as one of the components of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia was renamed into the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I suppose that the underlying cause was for this force to be the starting point of the future armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I joined the Ministry of Defence and when I assumed the duties that I have already described, my task became to -- in view of those units and the future armed forces that would be created, to draft the regulations that I've already mentioned. When we were drafting the law on the armed forces, which was a prerequisite for the existence of the armed forces, in one of its articles, Article 41, we expressly said, and I would like to quote something that I read yesterday afternoon again, therefore in Article 41 we said that until the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was fully established, its function will be performed by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now like to have a document with ERN number 0052760 handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe just an explanation here. I believe that an explanation should enter the transcript, referring to the exhibit. P286 refers to the decree law on defence. However, today we have seen the decree law on adoption of the law on the service in the armed forces. Are we going to say that P286 also includes the latter decree law? Later, as we discuss things, we may have difficulty in referring to this P286. So can we then consider that this decree law is part and parcel of this exhibit P286? I would like to draw attention to the fact that we are talking about two entirely different legal documents, two entirely different laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Defence counsel is correct. As a matter of fact, within P286 for clarification there is also a decision on the declaration of imminent threat of war, it also contains -- so that's certainly -- within our intention that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Does that satisfy you, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We might have had problems in subsequent use, the matter might have been confused if we had not clarified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is that we have on the record although the document itself speaks for itself, because once you go to it you realise that it is more than one document and one -- but anyway, I thank you both for raising this matter and for clarifying it. So let's proceed. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to ask Mr. Brkic to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number? Number? The number of document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It will be handed to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested under number 54, decree law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, is this the law that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here we have Article 41. However, I'm missing a page of the law here. A page is missing. The law is not complete. It's not complete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which number are you missing, sir? Which page number?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You're missing the page containing Articles 28 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If the usher could please assist. We understand that Article 28 is on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one is missing, this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: 00520761 at the bottom of the page we see Article 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely if you look at the two texts, the one in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but Articles from 28 to 43 are missing. Articles actually from 29 to 43 are missing from your version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is happening, Ms. Sellers -- what happened is this, that whoever stapled these together, after the second -- I'm referring to the B/C/S, after the second page of the government gazette, instead of putting the third page, which is page 155, they stapled page 156. So all we need to do is transpose the last page with the previous page, and there you find on the last page as stapled you get the sixth section of the law starting with Article 29 and then it finishes on that page, and we don't really need the next page, which is page 156, which has also been stapled. This is basically it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. For all intents and purposes for the time being, I would retain it because I don't know if there is a special reason why this has been inserted because it may come as a question or part of a question later on, if we are going to talk about law 55, 56 and 57. So leave it. But -- all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, first I'd like to draw your attention to Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just confirm for the Trial Chamber what was the intent of Article 1?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: To regulate the placement of all the armed and non-armed forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina under a single command, with a view to create the -- creating the legitimacy of these formations and creation of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina of all its nationalities as it says in Article 1, Muslims, Serbs, Croats and all the other members of other ethnic groups living together in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as to prescribe the ways the newly formed armed force would be commanded and controlled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to Article 2, and it says that in addition to the army that there is a police and armed units. Now, was the intent of Article 2 to bring these other additional units within what you've -- you have testified about as a unified command?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the intent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intent was to, under exceptional circumstances, when the combat situation dictated, that the Supreme Command could use certain police troops and other units such as customs and armed forces in companies, to place them under a single command of the command of the military unit in a territory in order to perform a certain combat task. Once this specific combat task was over, the police would return to its original strength within the Ministry of the Interior and the other armed units into their respective strengths. That is why you will have an order which -- I don't know whether you have amongst your exhibits, pursuant to which the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the Supreme Command resubordinated the reserve forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina and ordered them to carry out a certain set of tasks within a very critical period, the period in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was two points really. First, it was to the leading nature of the question and we can see that when it was rephrased is what was the intent we got a more realistic answer, and I would prefer it if my learned friend wouldn't suggest what the intents of legislation would be but merely ask. The second is a broader point - and I raise it now because it's probably going to surface throughout the course of this witness's testimony - is when we go on to talk about the intent of legislation, firstly, one only has recourse to what the intent was behind draftsmen and et cetera when the words are unclear; and secondly this witness obviously isn't the mouth of the oracle as to what the legislation means. In my country, we wouldn't go to the parliamentary draftsmen, we would go to Hansard and the debates of the legislature to see what legislation means. So it's merely to put that on the record, that this witness can talk about what he social security a draftsman had in mind, but of course that's not the last word as to what legislation means. That's for the legislature and the executive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely point taken, Mr. Jones, and as you know, in our system, when the law is still a draft bill, there you have at the end of the bill a declared intent and purpose behind each proposed legislation, which is then omitted when the bill becomes law, and as you say, we go back to the parliamentary debates and see from there. This case, the gentleman, the witness is -- happens also to be the person drafting. So what we should be seeking to obtain from him is whether, first of all, he had instructions, because I take it that at the time there was no really parliamentary system functioning when all this was happening. So we can't have recourse to parliamentary debates. That's number 1. Secondly, in other words, whether he had instructions from above or whether he was just taking the initiative and drafting laws without any direction from anyone. And he would then explain, I mean, if he had a direction or instructions, he would be able to tell us what the purpose behind the whole exercise was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think he also gave us a lot of information in answering the last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Might I just briefly return to the last question then I think we should answer Your Honour's question, and that is the clarification that he gave in Article 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it refers to the police and armed units, is that reference to the police reference to the military police or to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Civilian police only. In one of the regulations, the mention is made of the police, of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The military police is part of the armed forces already, so the military police don't have to be resubordinated as is separate unit. They are part of the military already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would ask to you please direct your attention to the question posed by the Trial Chamber. Would you please describe whether you had instructions or the purpose behind your drafting of these various laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that Madam Prosecutor is leading me or asking me leading questions, and that is why I would like to object, if I have the right to do that, to the objection put forth by the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor, let -- please allow us to be the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't try to take over our role. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. As I've already said - at the beginning, that is - of my own initiative and based on my knowledge, I drafted all the regulations in Bosnia and Herzegovina that refer to the armed forces, without any suggestions, proposals, recommendations, by anybody else, by any body. In other words, nobody determined any goals for me. They -- nobody provided me with any instructions. I was the most prominent person in the army by knowledge and by experience in that area. I had such an academic background that I was allowed to do all this on my own initiative, and I drafted all these laws based on my knowledge, and as the president of the Trial Chamber pointed out, this implied that every draft law or bill had to contain an explanation based on the constitution for drafting such a law. And this was done for the members of the government or the Presidency to help them why a law was being proposed in the version that was being proposed. This was an instruction for them, helping them to give their remarks, help -- to help them to either adopt or discard a certain draft of the future law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that sufficient? Would you want him to elaborate more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's not my witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In terms of the question you've asked, if you thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, more or less but I still have a big question mark on the overall scenario. I mean -- But someone would come to you and tell you, Professor or Dr. Brkic, we need a law on the armed forces of BiH, because otherwise you wouldn't sit down and start drafting a law just because you think it is -- it is -- it is or it has become useful. I mean, you would have or seek some direction from above because otherwise you would run the risk of creating a whole corpus of draft laws which nobody wants. So what was the situation? You are allowed a lot of free hand on how to draft these laws but you must have received some kind of direction. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time when I arrived at the Defence Ministry, which was the 13th of April, 1992, at that very time there was a meeting at the Defence Ministry attended by ministers from a number of different ministries. They were considering a draft law on Defence as a fundamental document that any country should have in order to ensure the security and defence of that country. I attended that meeting. That law was to be the fundamental basic law from which all further laws in relation to defence would then stem. Once -- when this law was adopted, it was submitted to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, as the legislative body that was adopted and passed this law on defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a fundamental document governing both defence and civilian protection, as well as reporting and civilian defence bodies. This was the cornerstone for all other provisions in the area of defence, including the law on the armed forces as well as other laws that were later to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That explains things a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brkic, can I ask you to go to Article 41 that you testified about earlier, now that the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel have that in front of them. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The meaning behind Article 41 was as follows. For the existing armed units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which since the 16th of April, 1992 had been transformed into the Territorial Defence units of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the word "socialist" having been deleted, the meaning was until they were organised, the armed forces were organised along proper lines, that the Territorial Defence units should act as the armed forces or in lieu of the armed forces, and that's why Article 1 of the law says the armed forces are made up by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then you asked me about the police and other armed units, but the obvious thing at the time was that on the ground we had no army but, rather, we had the TO units organised in terms of district and republican staffs. And all the provision that is were drafted were drafted for the benefit of the armed forces but the Article prescribes that until such time as a proper army is established, the function of the armed forces should be taken over by the Territorial Defence. And the same laws and prescriptions apply to the Territorial Defence at the time as would later apply to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In -- by way of corroboration, you have Article 36 of the same decree, saying that the 15th of April should be the day of the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 15th of April, 1992, the day the army was established, because that was the day when all armed formations existing in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were united under the Bosnia-Herzegovina TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do armed forces, armed formations, according to the legal documents, include the formations of the Territorial Defence at that time period?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No. None of the legal documents or provisions that were drafted under my supervision considered the Territorial Defence as an armed force. It was just the state of affairs at the time. But that was the reality on the ground. There were units around and we had to provide some sort of legal protection, and in a manner of speaking, legalise these units and organise them along some proper lines. And that is why this clause was included in the transitional provisions of the law, that until such time as a proper army was established, the TO would take over its role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic. I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We are finished with this exhibit, Your Honour and we would like to ask for a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document will be P543.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure, Ms. Sellers, this document does not already form part of the Official Gazette? Because I have a vague recollection that already we've had a government gazette or the first sets of government gazettes of Bosnia -- of the Republic of -- I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We had that with one of the expert witness testimonies. Your Honour, we did try --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to keep it separate, we will keep it separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That's fine. I think at this point we will keep it separate. Otherwise it will be confusing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, did there come a time when Bosnia-Herzegovina made a decision to declare a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the legal documents that inform the public of that decision to declare a state of war?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time decided on the 20th of June, 1992, or rather they were sitting in the office of one of the members of the Presidency, the president, this very -- this member of the Presidency that I have referred to, and I was present too, a decision was written to declare the state of war. I didn't draft this decision myself because this decision did not reflect my principles, technically speaking. It was written in the same form as a preamble by the United Nations General Assembly might have been, although the Minister of the Territorial Defence had earlier been adamant that a state of war should be proclaimed since there was fighting going on already in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and members of that Territorial Defence force were not to be envied in terms of their legal position. They were not guaranteed protection by the Geneva Conventions or any other set of laws that would give them legitimacy to wage war, or to be protected by the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether those groups were covered by the laws and customs of war at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: If you take as the starting point the fact that if you look at the Official Gazette 2/92 of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Criminal Code of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted as a Bosnia-Herzegovina law which, in chapter 16, I think that's Article 141, but I can't be certain, that's at least as far as my memory serves, defined criminal offences against the international law of war and the international law, genocide, war crime, that sort of thing. So if you look at the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it already contained some provisions of international humanitarian law, within the domestic legal system, and if you consider that, you can see that these provisions of the international humanitarian law were already being applied de facto, through these provisions that had been adopted from the former Yugoslav Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Ms. Sellers. Is this part that Ms. Sellers is dealing with or is addressing the witness to contested by the Defence? In other words, whether the existing law in BiH at the beginning of the war afterwards already contained provisions on what war crimes and humanitarian laws or not, because if it's not let's not waste much time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly the Defence doesn't contest that those provisions existed in the Criminal Code. What's more complex is what the witness was actually addressing a moment ago about whether particular formations enjoy the protection of international humanitarian law and obviously nothing is conceded on that front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic. I would concentrate on that, Ms. Sellers, rather than on what the Criminal Code contained because, first of all, we've heard ample evidence on that already. We have the copy of the Criminal Code itself plus other laws and so I would concentrate on what seems to be of more interest to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for that reason we have not produced the Criminal Code again as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I do want to clarify one point and that the application of the Criminal Code within Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time period, that that applied to persons in regards -- irrespective of whether they were members of the armed forces or any military formation, organised formation or civilians. Is that correct, Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the law existed, it wasn't specified who the law was to be applied to. It was to be applied to anyone who was guilty of committing a criminal offence. This is not a matter of personal jurisdiction, in terms of the relation between courts and perpetrators. This applied to everyone who was guilty of a criminal offence, and we can go back to Article 141. This person would have been taken to account for whichever crime he or she had committed; may have been murder or anything else. It's a question of lex specialis. The question was whether in a country -- and at the time this was Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I said, on the 15th of April, 1992 the law on military courts and military prosecutors was drafted as well as special courts, but it was not adopted at the time in order to transfer cases of personal jurisdiction to -- under the jurisdiction of special courts. At the time there were no such military courts, though, and this is the reason why the laws apply to all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina or anyone else who may not have been a citizen but was found -- was suspected of committing criminal offence in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to return to the question of whether the laws and customs of war applied to any armed formations or formations carrying out activity that could be considered combat during that time period, could you please address that?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're asking me whether the international conventions, the Geneva Conventions, or humanitarian conventions, were applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what your question about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could have been applied at that time.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind my experience as a lawyer, as a judge, as a former JNA officer, and knowing that this was the most important subject in all our military schools, that is international law and international law of war, our primary objective at the outbreak of clashes was to make sure that all standards of international humanitarian law and customs of war were being fully complied with, and that's why as part of this whole package of regulations, as far as concerned the Supreme Command, which was the supreme body in our military organisation, as early as the 23rd of August, 1992, I think, we drew up an order by the Supreme Command of the armed forces, the Supreme Command, regulating, as far as I can remember, and I believe it had four or five items only, so item 1 said that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be obliged to strictly and to the letter apply all the provisions of international law of war. One of the subsequent provisions was that all military commanders who are members of the armed forces were made responsible for compliance with the international provisions, and thirdly, that military commanders were responsible for training and informing their subordinate commanders and soldiers to fully comply with the provisions of international and humanitarian laws. And the next provision was, if I remember correctly, that all those who failed to comply with the provisions of the international humanitarian law and international law of war, their superiors would be entitled to -- and obliged to take steps against them. Pursuant to this order of the supreme staff that applied to the armed forces, a set of rules was written and other by-laws and decrees on the application of international law of war by the then Defence Minister and so on and so forth. I'm not sure if this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will be getting to that a little bit later in the direct examination. Going back to the 20th of June, you describe that there was a decision to declare a state of war. Was there also any issuance of a legal document concerning the public mobilisation within Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time period?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: At the same time as the decision to declare the state of war was produced, it was done by members of the Presidency, the same day I was given the task of writing the order for general mobilisation to apply throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I drafted this decision to the best of my ability, and as far as I remember it was at 12.00 that another member of the Presidency and I, facing TV cameras, and there was a lot of shelling going on around the building itself. This was the Bosnian railways building which is next to the Presidency, we read both these decisions, both the decision to declare a state of war and the decision for general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sellers, please. You said or I heard you say, I was given a task of writing the order for general mobilisation. Who gave you the order? Who gave you the -- who instructed you to draft this law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I name the person? Should I give you the name of the body, or should I give you the position of the person? Because the people present at the meeting of the Presidency were the late President Alija Izetbegovic, Fikret Abdic, Ejub Ganic. I'm not sure if anyone else was there, and I attended the meeting too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it they who gave you the instructions to draft --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness be given Prosecution Exhibit 278, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, if you could look at the decision to declare a state of war and then the following, the order to proclaim general public mobilisation in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and confirm to the Trial Chamber that these are the two decrees or decisions and orders that you've just testified about.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: These are two decisions. Firstly the decision to declare a state of war, which was drafted by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly the order to proclaim general public mobilisation in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that I drafted myself pursuant to a request by members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I please direct your attention to the decision to declare a state of war and, in particular, Article 4? In Article 4 we see mention of the provisions of international law, international conventions regulating the conduct of states in a state of war in conformity with Article 51 of the United Nations charter. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what types or which international laws and conventions that Article 4 implicitly refers to?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Well, the way we wrote laws, that would be Article 4 of this decision. This is in reference to the Geneva Conventions on how prisoners of war should be treated, on how the wounded should be treated. Those four conventions and other conventions from the area of humanitarian law that had already been ratified or were about to be ratified those very days by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is in reference to the application of the international laws and customs of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I would just briefly ask you to look at number 3, maybe I shouldn't say Article 3, the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is the reference to the armed forces consistent with your testimony earlier that the composition of the armed forces or armed organisations comprising of army and other possibly police units, is that phrase, "armed forces," consistent with your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The police of the interior ministry did not constitute the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what would that phrase be referring to in terms of groups, organisations or institutions?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: This sentence, rather this item, refers to the armed forces, meaning the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and until such time as this army is set up the reference is to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you now to look at the order to proclaim general public mobilisation in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and particularly under section 1, please. Now, Mr. Brkic, you drafted, if I understand correctly, this order and under section 1, we have in quotes "shall report" -- I'm sorry. "Between 18 and 55 years of age who shall report immediately to the nearest Territorial Defence unit with their military equipment and personal weapons." Would you please just tell the Trial Chamber what was the purpose of having people between 18 and 55 years report to the Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were a number of independent or illegal units as well as units or individuals who had left the former JNA. Not a great number of those, or at least not at that time. And the goal was to have this newly established staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have the Territorial Defence forces and all these armed units legalised and for them to be given the status of Territorial Defence units. There was a different decision saying that all those who failed to place themselves under the single command of the Territorial Defence would be considered illegal and that legal steps would be taken against them. Therefore, the objective was to gather all those who were carrying weapons, no matter whether military conscripts or not, all those aged between 17 and 65. The objective was for the -- all these people to be placed under a single command and system of subordination so that these people could not just go around doing whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand we are coming up on the break, and this would be an appropriate time period for me to break in this direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Brkic, we are going to have a short break now of about 25 to 30 minutes, during which we all have a meeting in my room. So we -- if the meeting doesn't finish within those 25 minutes there will be a short delay. We will try to stick to the 25 minutes but in case it takes us longer, please do understand. So let's break for 25 minutes. I think they will need assistance to be able to -- you look, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers. As you see, Professor, we took a little bit longer, as I had anticipated, but I'm sorry for that. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, we had been looking for over a document, it's P278 of the Prosecution exhibits but you would know it by the order to proclaim general public mobilisation in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would just ask you now to look under section 6 of the document and I have this highlighted in Sanction. And if you know, could you inform the Trial Chamber why the mobilisation order has stated that the commander of the Territorial Defence would be responsible for the -- its execution?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The practical execution of all the orders of the Supreme Command, according to the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was in the hands of the staff of the Territorial Defence and its commander, whoever it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we may remove the exhibit now from Mr. Brkic. Mr. Brkic, I would like to ask you whether you drafted or in any manner supervised a decree law on service in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I personally worked on drafting this law, given my previous experience and knowledge, and I knew that the service in the army had to be regulated, especially when it came to the officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilians working in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the purpose of the decree law on service in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the regulation of the armed forces, the members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose was to regulate the status of active members of the armed forces, namely generals, officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilians working in the BiH army. The concept of the army was to have its permanent staff or permanent employees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the date in which that decree was written or signed by the president?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can show him if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one further question prior to showing you the document, did you also participate in writing the rules of service in the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: No, not personally. One of my subordinates whose name was Sotirov Sota worked on that. I was just the coordinator. I made some corrections and then when these corrections were done, I was the one who authorised the use of these rules of service in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for a point of clarity, Mr. Brkic has pulled a document that he has in front of him. At this point -- yes, I just wanted to make sure that that was clear on the record. He is not consulting it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if, Mr. Brkic, you would just inform the Trial Chamber what document you have pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: This is a compilation of all the laws and regulations that I worked on and in which I participated as the author of the drafts or any -- in any other way. In other words, this is a compilation of the Official Gazettes that carried these regulations. This was a civilian gazette which was delivered to the armed forces to inform them of the shortened version of the legal texts that concerned them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, for the record we will be referring to Prosecution exhibits but just so it's clear I see that Mr. Brkic at times refers to his own personal copies of some of these rules and laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I take it that what he has held in his hands is nothing else but the -- some editions of the government gazette or Official Gazette, call it whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, you would confirm that; right?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: This is a compilation of all the official army gazettes issued in 1992 and in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the military Official Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If necessary, we will have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to have Mr. Brkic now shown the document bearing the ERN number 03091741. I'm sorry, 706.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is one of the new documents that you mentioned in the beginning of today's sitting, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. We will eventually have to ask for a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this the one that has not yet been translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is not the one that we referred to. Your Honour, for purposes of clarification, that's 03091706. I'll be referring to page numbers in the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I would ask you to look at the decree law on service in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the general provisions, Articles 1 through 5, please. If you could just briefly look at that. Now, I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber that the term armed forces during wartime, does that incorporate more than just members of the army?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The armed forces also comprise the military reservists, members of the reserve force, in addition to the army as the operative part of the armed forces during wartime or an imminent threat of a war. The way the armed forces are replenished is from the body of the reservists and conscripts, and all of these constitute the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could I draw your attention to Article 3. And is Article 3 consistent with the testimony that you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I said that the army is composed of generals, officers, non-commissioned officers, and civilians working in the army, namely those civilians who are employed by the BiH army. This law applies only to these four types of persons working in the armed forces. This law regulates their status, the way they are promoted. The way they are paid, their responsibilities, their health insurance, retirement, and other benefits, and let me just refer to the law to see if there is anything else. Health insurance, responsibility, pension, responsibility, working hours, and the way their service in the armed forces, in the active service of the armed forces, may be terminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you also is the term "armed forces" or person serving in the armed forces, is that analogous or is that the same or related to the term "servicemen"?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: When you say "analog," people serving or servicemen is an analog to those who are employed, who are employees in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at Article 3, the second sentence, that begins with: "Servicemen as defined by this decree."

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Active servicemen -- give me just a moment, please. I apologise, can you refer me again to the particular article?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 3, the second sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Active servicemen are non-commissioned officers, officers and generals and civilians serving in the army, are those civilians who are actively employed by the army. This means that the army is composed of generals, officers, non-commissioned officers and civilians who have been employed to work for the army. Here I am referring to some craftsmen or other types of personnel who do not necessarily have to have any military qualification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And the sentence above that, the second sentence in paragraph 1 of Article 3, just to slightly belabour the point, would you confirm that servicemen there also incorporate reserved forces?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: According to the second sentence in paragraph 1, active servicemen shall also include reservists or reserve members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to draw your attention to Article 5 of the decree. And if you would, please, comment to the Trial Chamber on the first and the second sentences of this Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: We are talking about commanders in the units. A commanding officer can be exclusively a military person, which excludes civilians from commanding posts. Civilians cannot command a unit. An exception to the rule is prescribed by paragraph 2 of the same article, where it says that exceptionally, the -- civilians who do not hold any rank can command a unit, and that is just an exception to the rule above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to draw your attention -- in the English it's page 38 of the document, the ERN number is 03091741, and it's the rules of service in the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you testified about earlier. Mr. Brkic, could you just briefly comment on what this legal document, the rules of service in the army, contain and the reason for their existence?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The rules of service is the code of conduct in the barracks or conditions similar to the barracks conditions, starting with the moment the soldiers get up in the morning to the moment when they go to bed in the evening. This regulates the service, the duties service, the sentry duty, honouring persons, and everything else that may take place in the course of one day in a military unit, in the course of the 24 hours that are in a day. This is the basic rule for regulating the life and work of a military unit in its barracks or in conditions similar to the life in its barracks. Some provisions also apply to the use of this unit during combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I ask you now to look at number 6, under the rules of service?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The same?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And if I might be permitted to just read that out into the record: "During combat operations, members of armed forces must adhere to the rules of international military law, to act humanely towards the wounded and the prisoners from the enemy ranks and protect the civilian population in accordance with international regulations and the constitution of the republic." Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what was meant or intended by international military law?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Since all the international conventions pertaining to the humanitarian law were at that time ratified by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in keeping with the rule on the application of the international humanitarian law, what was meant by this was to regulate the life of a soldier who found himself in combat. We wanted such a soldier to bear in mind at all times the application of international conventions and standards applicable during combat. And this implies at least four Geneva Conventions and two supplementary protocols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the phrase "international regulations," would you please tell the Trial Chamber what was intended by that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: In the classification of law, there are international standards and internal laws, and as far as I remember, one of the main provisions of the four Geneva Conventions, amongst other things, it says that from the moment the conventions are ratified by a state, they become legally binding in that state, and that the legislators of these countries have to incorporate within their internal laws the provisions of the conventions which in more specific terms regulate the areas that are regulated by these conventions, be it the prisoners of war, the treatment of civilians, of ill persons, of those who are wounded and every other provision that is regulated by the supplementary protocols. Obviously, we could not go into detail of all of that here. We just in very general terms said that our soldiers had to protect the international laws or the international humanitarian law. This is what this law was referred to even at our law schools. This is just a general duty binding upon all the servicemen and soldiers in accordance with the decision of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now ask you to turn to the last section, which is actually section 14, and underneath we have the name of the president and a date. Would you just confirm -- I'm sorry, in the English version, it's page 48. Just the date of the signing. That's what I'd like you to actually confirm.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't quite understand what you wanted me to confirm for you, the date when this was signed or...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just the date when this was signed as evidenced by the paper.

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: The date is 1st of August, 1992, and this document was signed by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the legislative body at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We can remove the document. I would like to ask if the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because since the very last article or section stated that these rules shall come into force on the day they are published in the Official Gazette of the Republic, do I take it that these rules that you've been testifying upon were published in the government gazette, in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army in its issue number 2 of the 5th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was published in Official Gazette 11/92, the Official Gazette of the government, that is. And I'm afraid I don't know the exact date when this was Official Gazette was actually published. However, judging by the exhibit that was given to me in its footnote it says that it was published in the Official Gazette of the government, issue number 11/92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And when was that? Can we establish the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll have to get back to you on the exact date of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can proceed with your next question. But please do come back to us on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, in your capacity during that time period, did you ever participate, either drafting or supervising, any rules or the manual on military discipline?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to give it a P number. That will be P544. Thank you, Judge Brydensholt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brkic, I'll repeat my question. Did you ever participate either drafting or supervising any rules or a manual on military discipline?

utterances.speaker: MUSIR BRKIC
utterances.text: I participated in the coordination and supervision of the drafting of this rule on military discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
